Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it doesn't see one word.

It sees *three pieces*.

---

**Tokenization** is the very first thing that happens to your prompt — before any "thinking" occurs.

The model doesn't read letters or words the way you do. It breaks text into chunks called **tokens**, which are roughly syllable-sized pieces, and converts each one into a number.

[EX]"unbelievable" → ["un", "believ", "able"] → [317, 6487, 1493] (approximate GPT-4 token IDs). The word "bank" is ONE token — but "I went to the bank" is five tokens, and the model has no idea yet whether "bank" means a riverbank or a financial institution.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only thing the model ever actually sees.[/KEY]

GPT-4 knows roughly 100,000 different tokens. Every prompt you've ever typed got silently sliced into pieces from that list before anything else happened.

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as input when you type a prompt?
A) A sequence of numbers representing token chunks
B) The exact words you typed, read left to right
C) A search query sent to a database
ANS: A
[/Q]

Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into ChatGPT, the model doesn't see that word at all.

It sees three chunks: **"un"**, **"believ"**, **"able"** — each converted to a number.

That's **tokenization** — the very first thing that happens the moment you hit send.

Every word (or word-piece) in your prompt gets sliced into tokens, and each token gets mapped to a number from the model's vocabulary. GPT-4 has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. Your entire prompt becomes a list of integers before the model does anything else.

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank" becomes something like [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] — five numbers, handed off to the next stage.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your text into a sequence of numbers — the only language the model actually speaks.[/KEY]

Here's the thing that trips people up: the model has no dictionary, no search engine, no database of facts. It never "looks up" your question. It only ever works with these number sequences.

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually do to your prompt before the model processes it?
A) It checks a database of correct answers
B) It breaks text into chunks and converts them to numbers
C) It searches the internet for relevant information
ANS: B
[/Q]

Here's a wild fact to kick us off:

The sentence "I went to the bank" contains a word that means completely different things — but to an early AI system, "bank" was just a number. No context. No disambiguation.

Just a token ID.

That's the problem **tokenization** was built around — and it's where everything starts.

---

When you type a prompt, the very first thing an LLM does is slice your text into **tokens** — chunks that are roughly word-sized, but not always.

"Unhappiness" might become three tokens: "Un", "happi", "ness." The word "cat" is one token. An emoji might be four.

GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of around 100,000 possible tokens.

[EX]Type the word "tokenization" into OpenAI's tokenizer tool and it splits into three pieces: "token", "ization" — each assigned a number like 3,642 or 89,201. The model never sees letters. It sees a list of integers.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only form an LLM can actually process.[/KEY]

---

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive when you type a prompt?
A) A list of numbers representing chunks of text
B) A search query sent to the internet

ANS: A
